name: Rafael Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Spanish and Portuguese into English, almost all medical: instruction manuals for devices like infusion pumps, patient leaflets, clinical trial forms. Most of it comes through one mid-size agency that's sent me work for five years. About six times a year I also interpret in the booth at medical conferences, which is the fun part. Otherwise it's me, two screens and a very long glossary at my kitchen table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is the conference days: two of us in a booth, swapping every half hour, and a surgeon talking way too fast. The worst is the manuals, honestly. Chapter seven of a pump manual is a lot like chapter seven of the last pump manual.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask a chatbot to build a first terminology list for a new device, then check every term against the regulator's database. I don't let it write the translation. My friend Dev, who also translates, uses it for everything, and I wait to see what goes wrong for him first.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how are things at home, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Comfortable. I live with my girlfriend Lena, who teaches at a primary school. I've got about eight months of costs saved and a bit in an index fund, which is a fund that just tracks the whole stock market. Medical work pays better than general stuff, so I'm on the higher side for translators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the hype dies down and it's a slightly better spellchecker. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for a year: useful for glossaries, not ready for patient safety. At the Thursday football I'd tell Dev he can stop sending me articles about the end of translation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I'd also know the manuals were always going to get cheaper. The agency already asks for a discount on repeated text. My conference days and the clinical trial forms would carry on as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agency and the conference work exactly as is. I'd take the agency's online course on their new translation memory tool, which stores past sentences for reuse, since they'll push it anyway. I'd raise my conference day rate a little next January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the version where I just get on with my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the manuals were always going to get cheaper. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but manuals are maybe a third of my work and the rate cut is slow. I'd rather lose some manual work than conference work. If anything I'd use the time to pitch to two more conference organisers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger translators doing general business documents. Their stuff is exactly the routine work that even a weak AI eats. I've got medical terms and a booth qualification behind me, and the younger translators have got neither.

say: I'd say AI is useful for **glossaries** but not ready for patient safety.
I'd tell my friend Dev to **stop sending** me end-of-translation articles.
think: The **manuals** were always going to get cheaper, with or without AI.
My **conference days** and clinical trial forms would carry on as they are.
do: Keep the **agency** and conference work exactly as they are.
Take the agency's course on its **translation memory** tool.
Raise the **conference day rate** a little next January.
feel: **Calm**, like the version where he just gets on with his career.
S0.quote: I've got medical terms and a booth qualification behind me, and the younger translators have got neither.
fieldNote: He separates **routine manuals** from conference work and sees only the first as cheapening.
He watches his friend **Dev** as a test case before adopting tools himself.
His worry goes to **junior translators** on general documents, not to himself.

steps.text: Keep the medical agency and six conference jobs a year
Pitch to two more medical conference organisers
Finish the agency's translation memory course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking. That's the manuals gone, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators need to become the people who check and sign off the machine's work, especially in medicine. I'd probably share a post about it, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my income drops by a third within two years. The agency will send manuals through a machine and ask me to review at half the rate. Conferences hold longer. Nobody wants a robot voice explaining a heart valve to a room of surgeons, but earpiece translation is creeping in anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the machine translation review workflow properly now, since it's clearly proven by then. I'd apply for in-house jobs at device makers in regulatory affairs, the people who check that every leaflet meets the rules. And I'd move a chunk of the index fund into plain savings, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd check job sites at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why in-house rather than staying freelance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because freelance is where the rate cuts land first. An in-house regulatory job has a salary, a pension and a team. It's less fun than the booth, but Lena and I want to buy a flat in a few years, and a bank likes a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there something you'd stop doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop taking the cheapest manual jobs entirely. If the rate's half, I'd rather spend those hours on applications. Dev would tell me I'm leaving money on the table, and he might be right.

say: I'd say translators must become the people who **check and sign off** machine work.
I'd post about **medical review** work, calmly, without drama.
think: My **income drops** by about a third within two years.
Conferences hold longer, but **earpiece translation** is creeping in there too.
do: Learn the **machine translation review** workflow properly.
Apply for in-house **regulatory affairs** jobs at medical device makers.
Move part of the **index fund** into plain savings.
feel: **Anxious**, checking job sites at night but not panicking.
S1.quote: Nobody wants a robot voice explaining a heart valve to a room of surgeons, but earpiece translation is creeping in anyway.
fieldNote: He expects a **one-third income cut** and moves toward a salaried job.
His plan is tied to **buying a flat** with Lena, which needs a steady salary.
He adopts AI review **once proven**, not before, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Learn machine translation review for medical manuals
Apply for regulatory affairs jobs at device makers
Shift part of the index fund into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's basically next year in translation terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to slow down and think about patient safety before hospitals trust any of it. People would roll their eyes, but someone has to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record: my job's finished. Everything I do is thinking work, and the regulatory job I'd be aiming for is thinking work too. The only thing I know that isn't on a screen is the medical devices themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big this month and pile the conference money into savings. I'd look at training as a field service engineer for medical devices, the people who go to hospitals and fix the pumps I translate the manuals for. That's hands-on, so it gets until about 2031, and I already speak the language of those manuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A cold feeling, like missing a step on the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is three extra years worth a whole career change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is three years of salary while I work out what's next, and repair work might hold a bit longer than the robots promise. It's not a forever answer. It's a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena the flat waits, and that her job is probably steadier than mine for once. She'd say we'll be fine, and she'd probably be right short term. But I'd hate being the one who's suddenly unsure.

say: I'd say hospitals should **slow down** on patient safety before trusting it.
I'd accept people **rolling their eyes** at that.
think: My **job's finished**, and the regulatory job I wanted is thinking work too.
The only thing I know that isn't on a screen is **the devices** themselves.
do: Freeze **big spending** this month and save all conference income.
Train as a **field service engineer** for medical devices.
Put the **flat purchase** with Lena on hold.
feel: **Alarmed**, a cold feeling like missing a step on the stairs.
S2.quote: The only thing I know that isn't on a screen is the medical devices themselves.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year robot gap** as a bridge, not a forever answer.
His device knowledge becomes the **way out**, from manuals to repair work.
He feels odd that his partner's teaching job is now the **steadier income**.

steps.text: Put all conference income straight into savings
Enrol in a medical device field service course
Pause buying a flat with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031, with robots around 2034. Okay, that's more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to move, while there's warning. I'd tell Dev and the younger ones at football to pick their next thing in the first two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get about three normal years, and then it's over for translation. The difference from the two-year one is that I can do the move properly instead of in a panic. I'd still go toward the devices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and booth work for now, at full pace, and save hard. In year two I'd start the field service engineer course part-time. I'd also ask the device makers I translate for whether they train their own engineers, since they know my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but it's the busy kind. I'd have a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save hard. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably half of what I earn from conferences, and nothing new on the index fund for a while. I want enough to cover a year of training on a low wage. Eight months now, I'd want fourteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booth. I'd miss the moment when a surgeon cracks a joke and I get the laugh in English half a second later. No repair job gives you that.

say: I'd say this is the time to **move while there's warning**.
I'd tell younger translators to **pick their next thing** in two years.
think: I get about **three normal years**, then translation is over.
I can make the move **properly** instead of in a panic.
do: Keep translating and **booth work** at full pace for now.
Start the **field service course** part-time in year two.
Grow savings from **eight to fourteen** months of costs.
feel: Anxious, but the **busy kind**, with a list to work through.
S3.quote: I'd miss the moment when a surgeon cracks a joke and I get the laugh in English half a second later.
fieldNote: With five years he plans an **orderly switch** rather than an emergency one.
He wants **fourteen months** saved to survive a year of low-wage training.
His real loss is **the booth**, the part of the job he loves.

steps.text: Keep full conference and translation workload until 2029
Start a part-time medical device repair course in 2028
Save half of conference income toward fourteen months' cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be 37. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same ending with better manners. Ten years is enough to retrain twice if you have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a good decade in medical translation and then have to leave it. With that much warning, I'd want to arrive at 2036 already doing something else, not still translating manuals in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Lena in the next two years, while I earn well, because property is something real. I'd keep translating, and around year four I'd retrain toward device repair or something else hands-on. Each year I'd look at what the first AI waves actually did before choosing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared, but it's still my whole job ending. It just ends slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the flat now rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because now I've got a strong income and a bank will lend to me. In 2034 I might be a trainee on half the pay. Lena agrees, she's been wanting it for ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once they're clearly reliable for medical text. I'd use them to take on more work in the good years and build up savings. If the end of translation is coming anyway, I'd rather the AI tools work for me first.

say: I'd say it's the **same ending** with better manners.
I'd say ten years is enough to **retrain twice** if needed.
think: I'd have **a good decade**, then have to leave medical translation.
I want to reach **2036** already doing something else.
do: Buy a **flat with Lena** within two years while income is strong.
Start retraining toward **device repair** around year four.
Use **reliable AI tools** to take on more work in the good years.
feel: Uneasy more than scared, but it's still his **whole job ending**, slowly.
S4.quote: If the end of translation is coming anyway, I'd rather the AI tools work for me first.
fieldNote: He uses the long runway to **buy property** before his income dips.
He'd **adopt AI tools** more readily here, as a way to earn more early.
He still expects his **job to end**, so the decade softens rather than removes worry.

steps.text: Buy a flat with Lena within the next two years
Retrain toward medical device repair around 2030
Use proven AI tools to take on more medical jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I can see a plan in the slower ones, but in two years I'd just be scrambling. What would help is cheap, quick technical training with a wage while you learn, and maybe device makers being made to hire people for hands-on support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about patients. When a translation of a pump manual is wrong, a nurse sets the wrong dose. I'd want someone checking that, whoever or whatever does the translating.

headlineQuote: When a translation of a pump manual is wrong, a nurse sets the wrong dose.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **medical translator**, Spanish and Portuguese into English, plus conference booth work.
He's **steady with technology**: he uses AI for glossaries and waits for proof before going further.
He has **eight months saved**, an index fund and a partner, Lena, who teaches primary school.
He moves from calm in **AI Plateau** to alarmed by AGI in two years.
His escape route is **device repair**, using the equipment he knows from the manuals.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd be scrambling instead of planning.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **technical training** with a wage paid while learning.
Device makers **hiring people** for hands-on support.
